title: Two hundred and forty thousand definitions of one anchor name, each used once
notes: The input is valid. A flow sequence holds the pair `&a 0, *a, ` two hundred and forty thousand times. Every `&a` gives the name `a` to a new node, and the alias after it refers to the most recent node with that name (section 3.2.2.2: an alias refers to the most recent anchor; section 7.1: an anchor may be defined again, and the alias before the next definition still means the earlier one). Every item is therefore the integer 0, 480,000 of them. A reader that looks a name up by scanning the earlier anchors of that name, or that keeps every definition in a list per name, does work that grows with the square of the number of definitions: 240,000 definitions are about 29 billion steps. A reader may also refuse the input with a limit error. The time limit is 50 seconds and is a hang guard, not a measure of cost. A linear reader needs about 1 second per megabyte, so about 3 seconds for this 2.4 megabyte input. A reader whose work grows with the square of the definitions takes longer than that, but one that finishes inside 50 seconds now passes: on time this case no longer separates quadratic readers from linear ones, and catches only a reader that hangs. The resource bounds are the robustness requirement of the kit, not a rule of the specification. The input is generated from the recipe in case.json (docs/case-format.md); the expected result is `[[0, 0, ...]]`, one document of 480,000 zeros, stored without spaces to stay under the size a stored file may have. Fast mode leaves this case out (tag `slow`); the full gate and a run with --slow include it.

provenance.reference: A reader that kept every definition of an anchor name in a list and searched it for each alias, so many definitions of one name took quadratic time.
